name: Supply Chain and Inventory Basics
objectives: Given your top five items, draw your supply chain and identify the weak spots, with a backup supplier or extra stock planned for each weak spot
Given one item you buy, compare three suppliers on landed cost, minimum order, lead time, payment terms and reliability, with a written quote from each and warning signs checked
Given an order to place, write a purchase order and check the delivery against it, with every problem written on the slip and reported the same day
Given your stock and your records, count your inventory and find the difference from your records, with every mismatch recounted by a second person
Given an item's daily use and lead time, calculate its safety stock and reorder point, getting the reorder point right with the formula
Using a free spreadsheet, build an inventory sheet that flags items to reorder, and plan how to keep first-in-first-out on the shelf, with the reorder point and status calculated by formulas

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Mapping your supply chain
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Draw your supply chain for your top items and spot where it could break.
This lesson builds toward: Given your top five items, you will draw your supply chain and identify the weak spots, with a backup supplier or extra stock planned for each weak spot.
A supply chain is every step that gets a product to your customer: the maker, any wholesaler or distributor, shipping, your shelf or storeroom, and finally the customer. Even a small business has one.
Start with your top five items: the ones that bring in the most money or that you cannot run without. For each, write who you buy from, how it gets to you, how long it takes, and where you keep it.
Then look for weak spots. Do you buy an important item from only one supplier? Does it come from far away? Does it spoil quickly? Is it seasonal? A weak spot is where you should keep extra stock or line up a backup supplier.
An AI assistant can help you brainstorm what could go wrong for each item, such as a supplier closing, a price jump or a shipping delay. You decide which risks are real for your business.
Step by step:
- List your top five items.
- For each, write the supplier, how it ships, how long it takes and where you store it.
- Draw arrows: supplier to shipping to you to customer.
- Circle weak spots: one supplier, long distance, spoils fast, seasonal.
- Write one fix for each weak spot.
Words to know:
- Supply chain: all the steps that get a product from the maker to your customer.
- Supplier: a business you buy goods or materials from.
- Wholesaler or distributor: a business that buys in bulk from makers and sells to other businesses.
- Weak spot: a step where something could easily go wrong.
Try it now: Draw the supply chain for your top five items on one page. Circle every weak spot and write one fix next to each, such as find a backup supplier or keep one extra week of stock.
You can now map your supply chain for your most important items and point out where it could break.

check.q: Which items should you map first?
options: Your top five items that bring in the most money or you cannot run without
Every item you have ever sold
Only items that are on sale
Items your competitors sell
check.why: Start with your top five items by money or importance.

check.q: Your key item comes from far away and spoils fast. What do you do?
options: Ignore it
Mark it as a weak spot and plan a backup supplier or extra stock
Stop selling it right away
Let AI decide which risks are real
check.why: A weak spot is where you keep extra stock or line up a backup supplier; you decide which risks are real.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Finding and comparing suppliers
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Find three possible suppliers for one item and compare them on more than price.
This lesson builds toward: Given one item you buy, you will compare three suppliers on landed cost, minimum order, lead time, payment terms and reliability, with a written quote from each and warning signs checked.
Places to find suppliers: makers and brands (ask who distributes in your area), wholesalers and distributors, trade shows, industry associations, local farms and makers, and other business owners in your field. Search online with the item name plus wholesale or distributor.
Compare on more than price. Look at the unit price, the minimum order quantity, lead time, shipping cost, payment terms, quality, and how reliable they are. Add shipping and fees to the price to get the landed cost, the real cost of each unit when it reaches you.
Ask each supplier for a written quote and, if you can, a sample. Ask other customers or check reviews. Keep at least one backup supplier for every important item.
Be careful with new suppliers that only accept wire transfers, gift cards or crypto, that have prices far below everyone else, or that rush you. Check their address and phone number, and start with a small order.
Step by step:
- List three possible suppliers for one item.
- Ask each for a written quote: unit price, minimum order, lead time, shipping and payment terms.
- Work out the landed cost per unit for each.
- Ask for a sample and check reviews or references.
- Choose a main supplier and a backup.
Words to know:
- Minimum order quantity (MOQ): the smallest order a supplier will accept.
- Lead time: the time from placing an order to having it in hand.
- Landed cost: the full cost of a unit when it reaches you: price plus shipping and fees.
- Payment terms: when you must pay, for example Net 30 means within 30 days.
- Quote: a written price offer from a supplier.
Try it now: Pick one item you buy. Find three possible suppliers and fill in a small table: unit price, minimum order, lead time, shipping, payment terms and landed cost per unit. Circle your main choice and your backup. Example: 100 units at $2.00 with $30 shipping is a landed cost of $2.30 a unit.
You can now find suppliers, compare them on landed cost, lead time, terms and reliability, and choose a main supplier and a backup.

check.q: Which is a good place to find suppliers?
options: A random social media ad promising free goods
Only the cheapest website you find
Trade shows and industry associations
Emails from strangers asking for gift cards
check.why: Trade shows, associations, wholesalers and other owners are good places to find suppliers.

check.q: A new supplier has a great price. What do you do before a big order?
options: Order a year's supply to lock in the price
Pay by wire right away
Skip the quote to save time
Get a written quote and a sample, check their address and phone, and start small
check.why: Ask for a written quote and sample, check them out and start with a small order.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Placing and checking orders
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a clear purchase order and check a delivery against it.
This lesson builds toward: Given an order to place, you will write a purchase order and check the delivery against it, with every problem written on the slip and reported the same day.
A purchase order (PO) is your written order to a supplier. It prevents mix-ups. It lists a PO number, the date, the supplier, each item with its code, the quantity, the price, the delivery date and address, and the payment terms.
When the delivery arrives, check it before you sign or put it away. Count the boxes and units, check that the items and sizes match the PO, look for damage, and check expiration dates on food or other goods that spoil.
Write any problem on the delivery slip and tell the supplier the same day, with photos. Do not pay for what you did not receive.
Keep each PO and its delivery slip and invoice together. Matching the three before you pay is called a three-way match, and it catches mistakes and overcharges.
Step by step:
- Write a PO with number, date, supplier, items, quantities, prices, delivery date and terms.
- When the delivery comes, count it and compare it with the PO.
- Check for damage and expiration dates.
- Write problems on the delivery slip, take photos and tell the supplier that day.
- Before paying, match the PO, delivery slip and invoice.
Words to know:
- Purchase order (PO): your written order to a supplier.
- Delivery slip: the paper that comes with a delivery listing what was sent.
- Invoice: the supplier's bill.
- Three-way match: checking the PO, delivery slip and invoice agree before paying.
Try it now: Write a sample purchase order for one item from your supplier table, with every part from this lesson. Then write a five-line checklist you will use the next time a delivery arrives.
You can now write a clear purchase order, check a delivery against it, and match the paperwork before you pay.

check.q: Which belongs on a purchase order?
options: Each item with its code, quantity and price
Your customers' names
Your bank password
Your sales goals
check.why: A PO lists the PO number, date, supplier, items with codes, quantities, prices, delivery and terms.

check.q: A box of yogurt arrives with expiration dates that have passed. What do you do?
options: Put it on the shelf quickly
Write it on the slip, take photos, tell the supplier that day and do not pay for it
Sign the slip and complain next month
Throw it out and say nothing
check.why: Check dates before signing, write problems on the slip and do not pay for what you did not properly receive.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Counting your inventory
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Do an accurate count of your stock and find the difference from your records.
This lesson builds toward: Given your stock and your records, you will count your inventory and find the difference from your records, with every mismatch recounted by a second person.
Inventory is the goods and supplies you have on hand. Your records say how much you should have; a count shows how much you really have. The difference is often called shrinkage: loss from theft, damage, spoilage or mistakes.
A full physical count means counting everything, often once or twice a year, when the business is closed. A cycle count means counting a few items each week, so every item gets counted over time. Count your most valuable or fastest-selling items most often.
To count well: give each item a SKU (a short code), count in the same unit you buy and sell in, count shelf by shelf, and have a second person recount anything that does not match. Write the count, the date and who counted.
Then compare your count with your records. Find out why big differences happened, and fix your records to match the real count.
Step by step:
- Give each item a SKU and a unit, such as each, box or pound.
- Choose a full count or weekly cycle counts.
- Count shelf by shelf and write the count, date and counter.
- Have a second person recount any mismatch.
- Compare with your records, find the reasons for big differences and update the records.
Words to know:
- Inventory: the goods and supplies you have on hand.
- SKU: stock keeping unit: a short code for each item you stock.
- Cycle count: counting a few items at a time on a regular schedule.
- Shrinkage: stock lost to theft, damage, spoilage or mistakes.
Try it now: Choose five items. Give each a SKU and a unit. Count them now and write the count, date and your name. If you have records, compare and write the difference for each.
You can now count your inventory accurately, run cycle counts and find shrinkage by comparing counts with records.

check.q: What is a full physical count?
options: Counting one shelf
Counting only expensive items
Counting everything, often once or twice a year
Guessing from sales
check.why: A full physical count means counting everything, often once or twice a year.

check.q: You find a big difference between your count and your records. What do you do after the recount?
options: Change the count to match the records
Ignore it
Delete the item
Find out why it happened and fix your records to match the real count
check.why: Find out why big differences happened and fix your records to match the real count.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Reorder point and safety stock
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate when to reorder an item and how much extra to keep.
This lesson builds toward: Given an item's daily use and lead time, you will calculate its safety stock and reorder point, getting the reorder point right with the formula.
The reorder point is the stock level that tells you to order again. If you order when you hit it, the new stock should arrive before you run out.
Reorder point = average daily use x lead time in days + safety stock. Example: you sell 10 bags of rice a day, and your supplier takes 4 days to deliver. Without any extra you need 10 x 4 = 40 bags to last until the order comes.
Safety stock is extra stock for surprises: a busy day or a late truck. A simple way: decide how many extra days to cover and multiply by daily use. With 2 extra days, safety stock is 10 x 2 = 20 bags. So the reorder point is 40 + 20 = 60 bags. When you get down to 60, order.
Keep more safety stock for items that matter most, items with long or unreliable lead times, and items you buy from one supplier. Keep less for items that spoil fast or cost a lot to hold. Check the numbers every few months, because sales and lead times change.
Step by step:
- Find the average daily use: units used over 30 days divided by 30.
- Find the lead time in days from your supplier.
- Choose extra days to cover and multiply by daily use: that is safety stock.
- Reorder point = daily use x lead time + safety stock.
- Recheck the numbers every few months.
Words to know:
- Reorder point: the stock level that tells you to order again.
- Safety stock: extra stock kept for surprises like busy days or late deliveries.
- Average daily use: how many units you use or sell on a typical day.
Try it now: For one item, find its average daily use and lead time. Choose extra days of cover. Work out the safety stock and the reorder point and write them on a card you keep by that item.
You can now calculate the reorder point and safety stock for an item and know when to keep more or less extra.

check.q: You use 6 units a day and want 3 extra days of cover. What is the safety stock?
check.why: Safety stock is extra days times daily use: 3 x 6 = 18.

check.q: Your supplier's lead time grows from 4 days to 8 days. What do you do?
options: Keep the same reorder point
Recalculate the reorder point with the new lead time
Stop using safety stock
Order only when you run out
check.why: Check the numbers when lead times change, because the reorder point depends on them.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: A spreadsheet inventory and first-in-first-out
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a spreadsheet that flags items to reorder and keep stock moving first-in-first-out.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free spreadsheet, you will build an inventory sheet that flags items to reorder, and plan how to keep first-in-first-out on the shelf, with the reorder point and status calculated by formulas.
A free spreadsheet, such as Google Sheets or Microsoft Excel on the web, can run a small business's inventory. Make one row per item and these columns: Item, SKU, Main supplier, Backup supplier, Unit cost, On hand, Daily use, Lead time (days), Safety stock, Reorder point and Status.
Let the spreadsheet do the math. If Daily use is in column G, Lead time in H and Safety stock in I, the reorder point in J2 is =G2*H2+I2. The status in K2 can be =IF(F2<=J2,"REORDER","OK"), which shows REORDER when on hand (column F) is at or below the reorder point. Copy the formulas down. Update On hand after each count or delivery.
First-in-first-out (FIFO) means you sell or use the oldest stock first. It keeps food and other goods from expiring at the back of the shelf. When new stock arrives, put it behind or under the older stock, and label boxes with the date received.
An AI assistant can help you write or fix a spreadsheet formula. Describe your columns in words; you do not need to share your supplier prices or other private business data.
Step by step:
- Open a free spreadsheet and add the eleven column headings.
- Fill in five items.
- In the Reorder point column, enter =G2*H2+I2 and copy it down.
- In the Status column, enter =IF(F2<=J2,"REORDER","OK") and copy it down.
- Update On hand after each count or delivery.
- On the shelf, put new stock behind the old and date-label each box.
Words to know:
- Spreadsheet: a grid of rows and columns that can do math for you.
- Formula: an instruction in a spreadsheet cell that calculates a result, starting with =.
- First-in-first-out (FIFO): using or selling the oldest stock first.
Try it now: Final task: build your inventory spreadsheet for five items with all eleven columns, the reorder point formula and the REORDER flag. Then write two sentences on how you will keep first-in-first-out on your shelf.
You can now run a simple spreadsheet inventory that flags when to reorder and keep stock moving first-in-first-out.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Items and suppliers Items are missing a SKU, unit cost or main supplier. Five items, each with SKU, main supplier, backup supplier and unit cost. Unit cost is the landed cost including shipping and fees. Stock and use numbers On hand, daily use or lead time is guessed or missing. On hand comes from a real count, with daily use and lead time filled in. Notes the count date and who counted. Reorder point and safety stock Reorder point is typed in by hand or calculated wrong. Safety stock set and reorder point calculated with a formula for every item. More safety stock is kept for key or single-supplier items, with a reason. Reorder flag No status column, or it does not change when stock is low. Status shows REORDER when on hand is at or below the reorder point. The learner tests it by changing On hand and checking the flag. First-in-first-out plan No plan for rotating stock. Written plan to date-label boxes and put new stock behind the old. Names who does it and when, such as on every delivery. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: In this lesson's sheet, what does =G2*H2+I2 calculate?
options: The unit cost
The status
The reorder point
The number of suppliers
check.why: Daily use times lead time plus safety stock gives the reorder point.

check.q: You want AI to help fix a spreadsheet formula. What do you share?
options: Your supplier prices and bank details
Your whole customer list
Your login password
A description of your columns in words
check.why: Describe your columns; you do not need to share prices or private business data.
